newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-DePfa surges on UBS takeover talk.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-DePfa surges on UBS takeover talk.

text.p: Shares in German mortgage lender DePfa-Bank AG soared on Tuesday after it inadvertently put itself on the map as a takeover candidate, saying it believed Swiss giant UBS may have amassed a nine percent stake.
But Union Bank of Switzerland denied the statement and insisted its stake in DePfa was less than one percent. It added that it had no intention of taking over the bank.

DePfa's shares surged as much as 13 percent to an all-time high of 91 marks after the bank said inquiries by an independent firm indicated UBS had bought a "substantial part" of its capital in the open market.

The news spurred speculation that UBS may be seeking a controlling stake in the German bank, seen as an attractive target in view of its strength in the European market for public loans and its position as a leading German debt issuer.

But confusion reigned and much of DePfa's share gains were lost after UBS issued a firm denial of the takeover rumours, saying an acquisition of DePfa "would not fit at all" into its strategic plans. DePfa's shares closed at 86.50 marks.

Under a new chief executive since last year, UBS has set its eyes firmly on expanding in the lucrative area of asset management -- a field in which DePfa is not active -- while trimming more costly businesses, chiefly retail banking and corporate lending.

Chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta last month said part of this strategy was likely to include acquisitions but limited the scope of interest to asset management and private banking operations, especially in the U.S.

DePfa itself said talk of a takeover bid would be "pure speculation" but a spokesman added that the bank, as a leading leading provider of state financing across Europe, may be interesting for a Swiss bank preparing for monetary union.
While no final clarification was immediately available on Tuesday, some analysts said a takeover of DePfa may make sense.

Konrad Becker, banking analyst at Merck, Finck in Duesseldorf, said, "I don't know if UBS will launch a takeover bid but I could imagine it. DePfa has now been put on the map as a takeover candidate, it wasn't regarded as one before."

Wiesbaden-based DePfa, short for Deutsche Pfandbrief- und Hypothekenbank AG, was strong in the low-risk business of lending to governments and a takeover would give UBS better access to the German debt market, Becker said.
DePfa has a market capitalisation of about three billion marks ($1.8 billion) and total assets of about 165 billion marks. It does not engage in retail banking.

The bank refinances itself by issuing debt and issued 32 billion marks in bonds last year. It is Germany's biggest issuer of Pfandbrief bonds -- bonds issued to refinance mortgages or public projects.
Some 60 percent of its capital is widely distributed while the remaining 40 percent is owned by a holding company, DePfa-Holding Verwaltungsgesellschaft mbH.
DePfa's surprise announcement came in a mandatory statement on Tuesday morning.
A spokesman said the bank had asked a company specialising in identifying shareholders to conduct checks after a market participant had noticed "certain concentrations" in its share ownership.
DePfa had on Monday asked UBS for a written comment after the investigation led it to believe UBS held nine percent.

The Swiss group on Monday night responded that its examination of its holdings in Europe revealed a stake of less than one percent. Further checks of its global bond holdings on Tuesday led to the same conclusion, UBS said.

Analysts said the confusion may stem from an 8.2 percent stake in DePfa held by Swiss insurer Swiss Life. UBS will own 25 percent of Swiss Life if the insurer gains approval for a planned conversion into a listed company on June 30.
($ = 1.705 German Marks)
